clinicalPearls: Hard metal is a sintered composite of tungsten carbide with a cobalt binder used for cutting tools, drill bits and wear-resistant parts; cobalt is the principal skin sensitiser.
Workers in tool grinding, sharpening and manufacture present with hand and forearm eczema, and diamond polishers using cobalt-containing wheels are a classic at-risk group.
The dermatitis is usually an allergic contact dermatitis to cobalt, though irritant contact dermatitis from coolants, abrasives and wet work frequently coexists and can be hard to separate.
Cobalt allergy commonly occurs together with nickel and sometimes chromate sensitivity, so concurrent reactions on patch testing are frequent.
Wet grinding coolants both leach cobalt from the workpiece and act as irritants, increasing skin exposure and barrier damage.
The same cobalt exposure can cause hard metal lung disease (giant-cell interstitial pneumonitis) and occupational asthma, so enquire about respiratory symptoms.
Patch testing to cobalt chloride, nickel sulfate and potassium dichromate is central to diagnosis; workplace and glove assessment complements it.
Management combines cobalt avoidance and substitution, improved coolant hygiene, appropriate gloves and barrier care, and treatment of the eczema.
reference.pathophysiology: Hard metal dermatitis is predominantly a delayed-type (type IV) hypersensitivity to cobalt. Cobalt ions released from the alloy — especially when wet-grinding coolants leach metal from tools — penetrate the epidermis and bind host proteins to form haptens that are processed by Langerhans cells and presented to T lymphocytes; on re-exposure a sensitised T-cell response produces spongiotic eczematous inflammation. Superimposed irritant contact dermatitis is common, driven by coolants, solvents, abrasive dusts and repetitive wet work that damage the stratum corneum barrier, enhance penetration of allergens and lower the threshold for both irritant and allergic reactions. Frequent co-sensitisation to nickel and chromium reflects shared exposures and possibly cross-reactivity. Inhaled cobalt-tungsten carbide particles can additionally provoke immunologically mediated interstitial lung disease and asthma through separate respiratory mechanisms.
additionalDifferentials: irritant contact dermatitis from coolants and wet work
allergic contact dermatitis to nickel or chromate
allergic contact dermatitis to biocides or additives in metalworking fluids
additionalInvestigations: detailed occupational history of grinding, coolants and materials handled
patch testing to cobalt chloride, nickel sulfate and potassium dichromate
patch testing to metalworking fluid components and biocides
assessment and testing of coolants and gloves used in the workplace
skin swabs if secondary infection of eczema is suspected
respiratory enquiry with spirometry or peak-flow monitoring if symptomatic
chest imaging and specialist referral if hard metal lung disease is suspected
redFlags: breathlessness or cough suggesting hard metal lung disease or occupational asthma
severe or widely spreading eczema with signs of secondary infection
rapid recurrence on return to work indicating uncontrolled exposure
involvement of multiple co-workers implying a systemic hygiene failure
features suggesting systemic contact dermatitis from ingested or inhaled cobalt
reference.prognosis: With cobalt avoidance, improved coolant hygiene and barrier measures the dermatitis often improves, but established cobalt sensitisation is lifelong and eczema may persist or recur if exposure continues. Coexisting respiratory disease worsens the overall outlook and warrants separate management.
pitfalls: Attributing the eczema solely to irritation and missing underlying cobalt allergy.
Testing only for nickel and overlooking concurrent cobalt and chromate sensitivity.
Ignoring respiratory symptoms and failing to consider hard metal lung disease.
Assuming gloves are protective without checking permeation and hygiene practices.
Overlooking coolant biocides and additives as separate sensitisers or irritants.
references: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, current edition
Adams' Occupational Skin Disease, current edition
management: Eliminate cobalt exposure through substitution, improved coolant hygiene, and engineering controls, as avoidance is the definitive treatment
Restore and protect the skin barrier with emollients, suitable protective gloves, and reduction of wet work
Treat eczematous flares with topical corticosteroids, reserving short courses of systemic steroids for severe disease
Address coexisting irritant contact dermatitis by minimising contact with metalworking-fluid coolants, solvents, and abrasive dusts
Confirm and characterise sensitisation with patch testing to cobalt, nickel, and chromate to direct avoidance
Enquire about and screen for associated respiratory disease such as occupational asthma and hard metal lung disease
Refer to occupational health for workplace assessment, and escalate to task modification or redeployment where dermatitis persists despite exposure
